name: The Lahaina Banyan Tree

location.address: Lahaina Banyan Court Park, corner of Front Street and Canal Street, Lahaina

access: The park has been closed to the public since the August 2023 wildfire; a perimeter fence keeps visitors back from the tree and the burned-out Old Lahaina Courthouse beside it, with signs warning against trespassing. As of the Feb 2026 source, the tree and benches are visible from the fence line and from Front Street; a full arborist health assessment was pending, and county officials hoped to reopen the park before the end of 2026 if it proved safe.
transport: In central Lahaina, on Front Street opposite the small boat harbor
verify_notes: Planted 24 April 1873 by sheriff William Owen Smith, a gift seedling from missionaries in India, to mark the 50th anniversary of the first American Protestant mission in Lahaina. By 2005 it had grown to 16 trunks, ~49ft tall, with an aerial-root canopy spanning 0.66 acres and a 0.25-mile circumference (this is the canopy spread, not a trunk girth). Register (Hawaii Exceptional Trees, row 992) gives a trunk girth of 1200.9cm / diameter 382.5cm / height 56.5ft as of its assessment, described there as 'Excellent' vitality pre-fire; treat that figure as a buttressed multi-trunk mass rather than a single stem. It is the largest banyan tree in Hawaii and one of the largest in the US. The 8-9 Aug 2023 wildfire burned through Lahaina; the courthouse beside it was destroyed but the fire 'skipped right over the park' per Maui County arborist Timothy Griffith. About 40% of the tree's canopy/branches had to be removed afterward due to fire damage (dessication, 'superheating' near Front/Hotel Streets). A Feb 2026 Civil Beat piece (Erin Nolan) reports arborists found fungus in a branch that snapped that month and an extensive invasive health assessment (tension tests, cambium checks) was being organized, not yet scheduled; 'we really don't know what's under the skin' (Duane Sparkman, Maui County Arborist Committee chair). The tree is alive and standing as of that report; long-term prognosis is genuinely uncertain, hence flagged rather than a clean bill of health. Worth flagging to the writer as a story of survival-in-progress rather than a triumphant recovery.

name: The Ka'ahumanu Church Monkeypod

location.address: Ka'ahumanu Church, 103 South High Street, Wailuku

access: Free. On the grounds of a working historic church (the oldest continuously used stone church on Maui, fourth building on the site, built 1875), open during daylight hours; the tree stands in the churchyard along High Street.
transport: In central Wailuku, on South High Street
verify_notes: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (row 989) lists this monkeypod at 'Ka'ahumanu Church', vitality Excellent, girth 835.2cm / diameter 264.2cm / height 36ft. The church's own site describes its grounds as 'surrounded by the monkeypod, the kukui, the mango and the kou trees', and a local community page (Wailuku Community Helping Hands, Facebook) separately references restoration/pruning work on 'the Ka'ahumanu historical church's monkeypod tree', in the singular, suggesting one standout specimen rather than several equal candidates, but I could not get tree-level coordinates within the church lot, only the church's own address, hence approximate. Ka'ahumanu Church, built in 1875 (fourth structure on the site since 1832), is outside the Lahaina burn zone, in Wailuku. No documented planting date or reliable species-specific girth growth-rate found in the time available, so age is left blank rather than guessed; a monkeypod (Samanea saman / Albizia saman) is fast growing and estimates vary too widely without a solid regional growth-rate figure. Register's `girth_unit_check: ok`.

name: The Kalana Pakui Banyan

location.address: Kalana Pakui Building (former police station), 250 South High Street, Wailuku

verified_sources: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register, row 988 (State of Hawaii DLNR Division of Forestry and Wildlife, CC0)
access: Free. On the grounds of a public county government building (built 1925 as the police station, now county offices) in the Wailuku Civic Center Historic District; visible and reachable from the street and the building's public lawn.
transport: In central Wailuku, on South High Street
verify_notes: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (row 988) lists this Indian laurel fig at 'Kalana Pakui Building', vitality Good, girth 1094.2cm / diameter 348cm / height 53ft, owner listed as Maui County. The Kalana Pakui Building (Wikipedia: Wailuku Civic Center Historic District) was built 1925, designed by William D'Esmond, originally the police station, now county offices at 250 South High Street. This is a second independent source for the SITE (existence of the building and its public, government-owned grounds) but not a tree-specific source beyond the register; I could not find a second source naming this specific tree in the time available, so it is flagged rather than fully corroborated, and the pin is approximate (register grid plus the building's street address, not a tree-level fix). No documented planting date or age found; leaving age blank rather than guessing. Register's `girth_unit_check: ok`. Worth a second look by a later pass for photo/street-view confirmation of the tree against the building.

name: The Honoapi'ilani Highway Kiawe

location.address: Honoapi'ilani Highway, oceanside near mile marker 11, between Ma'alaea and Olowalu

verified_sources: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register, row 1119 (State of Hawaii DLNR Division of Forestry and Wildlife, CC0)
access: Free, on state Department of Transportation land beside a public highway; the register itself records it as 'Visible from Street/Accessible'. Only the register's grid coordinates and the mile-marker description are available, so the pin is approximate; a later pass should confirm the exact roadside spot.
transport: By car on Honoapi'ilani Highway (State Route 30), West Maui coast
verify_notes: Only source found is the Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (row 1119): girth 810.8cm / diameter 259.1cm / height 30ft, vitality Good, owned and located by the State of Hawaii Dept. of Transportation, locality 'Honoapiilani Highway, near Mile Marker 11 oceanside', accessibility explicitly recorded as 'Visible from Street/Accessible'. Kiawe (Prosopis pallida, a mesquite introduced from Peru in 1828) is one of the largest and oldest kiawe recorded on Maui by girth. I could not find a second independent source (news, iNaturalist, local blog) confirming this specific tree within the time available; general web search tools were rate-limited/bot-blocked during this pass (DuckDuckGo lite returned an anti-bot challenge page, Bing's results were not query-relevant). Flagged for a single-source register entry; a future pass with working search tools or a drive-by photo could confirm and upgrade the pin. No age given by the register and no growth-rate figure found in time; left blank rather than guessed.
